answer.reason: This single-worker pool only ever gets one call. When shutdown runs, that call has either finished, been cancelled already by future.cancel(), or is running, and cancel_futures cannot stop a running call. So the flag never has a queued item to act on, and the timeout, fallback and shutdown behaviour do not change.

answer.reason: When no attempt timeout is configured, the mutant returns None without ever calling the executor, so every sync request without a timeout silently gets no response. The timeout handling is only meant to change behaviour when a timeout is set; with no timeout, the attempt must run on the current route and return its result.
answer.test_focus: Send a sync request with no attempt timeout set (timeout_seconds is None) and check that the executor is called and its actual LLMRouterResponse comes back, not None.

answer.reason: The mutant drops the pool shutdown, but the caller still stops waiting after the timeout, raises the same TimeoutError and returns the same result on success. What changes is only how long idle worker threads live and when the pool is cleaned up, and no requirement asks about that.

answer.reason: Once the timeout fires, the future is normally already running on the single worker, so future.cancel() does nothing. If the call hasn't started yet, pool.shutdown(cancel_futures=True) in the finally block cancels the queued work anyway. Either way the TimeoutError is raised straight away, so waiting, fallback and the terminal timeout all behave the same.

answer.reason: After a timeout, the mutant leaves timed_out False, so the finally block calls pool.shutdown(wait=True) and blocks until the timed-out executor call finishes. The sync path therefore keeps waiting on the timed-out route, against the requirement that it stop waiting. The existing tests likely pass only because their slow executor returns soon anyway.
answer.test_focus: Use a sync executor whose first route blocks on an event that is only released after the test's assertions. Check that the request falls back to the second route and succeeds, or raises TimeoutError when no fallback remains, within a bounded time well below the blocked call's duration.

answer.reason: On timeout the mutant calls pool.shutdown(wait=True), and this runs in the finally block before the TimeoutError propagates. So the sync path keeps blocking until the hung executor call finishes. That breaks "stop waiting on the current route": fallback, or the timeout error, is delayed for as long as the slow route runs, and forever if it never returns.
answer.test_focus: Use a sync executor whose first route blocks on an event that is only released after the assertion, or that sleeps well past the timeout. Check that the request falls back to the next route, or raises the timeout, within about timeout_seconds and before the blocked call returns.

answer.reason: The only difference is the starting value of timed_out, which matters only when the attempt does not time out. By then future.result() has finished, so shutting down without waiting just skips joining an idle worker thread. The returned response, the raised errors, the timeout and the fallback all behave the same.
